To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
inferring diet from functional classifications rather from direct diet assessment can lead to erroneous conclusions about stoichiometry and its consequences.

inferring the diet from functional feeding guilds results in inaccurate estimates of the stoichiometry of consumer–resource interactions, and that these errors are likely to be greatest when consumers are most likely to respond to changes in resource stoichiometry by altering their diets.
the elemental imbalances (N:P and C:P) between consumers and resources were significantly lower when estimated from the realized diet than from the inferred diet.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the stoichiometric constraints imposed by food on consumers, and how these constraints may be affected by the diet of consumers.
the stoichiometry of consumer–resource interactions, specifically the imbalances that arise when the supply of elements in resources is insufficient to satisfy the demand from consumers.
understanding the role of the elemental composition of resources on the elemental composition of their consumers, and the consequences of such imbalances for consumers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, while the inferred diet may be a useful starting point, it is the realised diet that is important in terms of stoichiometric constraints.

, for the systems considered in this study, the inferred elemental imbalance is not an appropriate measure for the stoichiometric constraint on the consumer, as the realised elemental imbalance is much smaller.
the elemental imbalances between the consumer and its food are not as great as those inferred from functional feeding groups.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the diet of the consumers is more important than their functional guild in determining the elemental imbalances of consumers with their resources.

inferring the diet from feeding guild is a poor approximation of the real diet of consumers, and that this can have significant consequences for the interpretation of the ecological significance of stoichiometry.
the stoichiometric imbalanaces between the diet and the resource were smaller than the imbalances between the functional feeding group and the resource.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the elemental imbalances between consumer and resources should be calculated using the actual diet of the consumer, which may be more plastic than previously assumed, rather than inferring diet from functional classification of the species concerned.
the diet inferred from functional feeding guilds is not necessarily representative of the diet of the consumers.
it is essential to determine the diet of consumers directly, and to avoid using functional guilds to estimate the elemental composition of consumer diets.
